What happens when the clean energy technologies we deploy today reach the end of their lives?
 
By 2050, the world could generate up to 78 million tonnes of retired solar panels. Recycling energy transition minerals could reduce the need for new mining by 25-40%, while creating a $200 billion global market. Yet circularity remains an overlooked—and key—part of the energy transition.
 
Today, I had the privilege of delivering the opening remarks and keynote at the UN High-level Political Forum side event, Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa, alongside colleagues and partners from across the public and private sectors.
 
Circularity isn't just about managing waste. It's about designing energy systems from the start to maximize the value of every clean energy investment.
 
Three takeaways stood out:
•⁠  ⁠Circularity is an industrial opportunity. Repair, remanufacturing, recycling, and second-life applications can create jobs, strengthen local industries, and capture more value from the energy transition.
•⁠  ⁠Digitalization is an enabler. From battery passports and AI-assisted mineral discovery to smart grids that could reduce the continent's estimated $5 billion in annual transmission and distribution losses, data is becoming the backbone of circular energy systems.
•⁠  ⁠Regional cooperation is essential. Integrated regional value chains, from critical minerals and manufacturing to repair, second-life use, and recycling, will be key to scaling circular industries.

As renewable and off-grid solar continue to expand across Africa, we have an opportunity to build energy systems that are circular, resilient, and designed to deliver long-term development benefits.
 
Thank you to all the organizers, speakers, and participants for an engaging discussion.
